steps: ICU; beta-blocker (propranolol) for adrenergic symptoms and to block T4→T3 conversion.
Antithyroid drug — propylthiouracil (preferred in storm) or carbimazole.
Give iodine (Lugol's/potassium iodide) at least 1 h AFTER the antithyroid drug.
Hydrocortisone (reduces T4→T3 and treats relative adrenal insufficiency).
Supportive: cooling, fluids, treat the precipitant (often infection); avoid aspirin.

drugRefs.dose: 60–80 mg PO every 4–6 hours (or 0.5–1 mg IV slowly, repeated with cardiac monitoring)
drugRefs.why: Controls the hyperadrenergic state (tachycardia, tremor, agitation) and, at high dose, blunts peripheral T4→T3 conversion.

drugRefs.dose: 500–1000 mg loading, then 250 mg every 4 hours
drugRefs.why: Blocks new thyroid hormone synthesis and, unlike carbimazole, also inhibits peripheral T4→T3 conversion — preferred in the acute crisis.
Alternative thionamide blocking hormone synthesis when propylthiouracil is unavailable or contraindicated.

drugRefs.dose: Lugol's iodine 5–10 drops (or potassium iodide) every 6–8 hours
drugRefs.why: Inhibits release of stored thyroid hormone. Must be given at least 1 hour AFTER the antithyroid drug, otherwise it can fuel further hormone synthesis.

drugRefs.dose: 100 mg IV every 8 hours (or 300 mg loading then 100 mg 8-hourly)
drugRefs.why: Reduces peripheral T4→T3 conversion and covers the relative adrenal insufficiency of severe thyrotoxicosis.

refs: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine, 22e — Hyperthyroidism and Thyrotoxicosis
ATA Guidelines for Diagnosis and Management of Hyperthyroidism and Thyrotoxicosis

confirm: Severe thyrotoxicosis with fever, tachyarrhythmia, agitation/delirium, GI/hepatic dysfunction (Burch-Wartofsky score). Treat clinically.
